bp: Peer review is the gatekeeping system behind scientific publishing: reviewers read a submitted paper, judge whether its claims are sound, and give authors advice about what must be fixed. That system only works when reviews are careful, specific, fair, and useful to editors. The pressure behind PeeriScope is that scholarly venues now handle review work at a scale where quality varies widely and manual checking is hard. An editor may need to understand not just whether a review is positive or negative, but whether it gives evidence, follows a rubric, explains its reasoning, and helps the decision process. PeeriScope serves that practical need by treating review quality as something that can be inspected across several dimensions. The paper presents it as a modular platform with a public interface and API, aimed at reviewer self-assessment, editorial triage, large-scale auditing, and continued research on how review quality should be measured.
wh: The hard part is that a good review is not just a long review, a polite review, or a review with a confident recommendation. Review quality is made of several partly overlapping judgments: whether the reviewer addresses the paper's substance, whether comments are constructive, whether the reasoning follows a stated rubric, and whether the review gives editors enough signal to act. A simple automatic checker can count visible features, but many important qualities live in meaning, not only in surface form. A language model can read the text more flexibly, but its judgment can be difficult to trust unless it is guided and made interpretable. A trained predictor can learn from past examples, but it may hide why a review was flagged. PeeriScope is hard because it has to support practical deployment while keeping the assessment systematic, interpretable, and extensible instead of becoming one opaque quality score.
naive: A smart beginner would build a checklist: count review length, count whether strengths and weaknesses are mentioned, look for harsh words, and flag reviews below a threshold. That would catch some shallow reviews, but it would miss the central problem. A long review can still misunderstand the paper, and a short review can sometimes identify one decisive flaw. A checklist also freezes one venue's idea of quality, even though rubrics and editorial needs differ. Another beginner move would be to ask a language model for a single quality score. That may read more nuance, but without a rubric, structured features, or trained prediction, the score is hard to audit and hard to integrate into editorial workflows.
ap: PeeriScope's central move is to split review-quality evaluation into cooperating parts instead of trusting one measurement. It integrates structured features, rubric-guided language-model assessments, and supervised prediction. The structured features capture inspectable facts about the review that can be logged and compared. The rubric-guided model assessment asks a language model to judge quality along defined dimensions, so the judgment is tied to explicit criteria rather than a vague impression. The supervised prediction layer uses examples to learn which patterns are associated with quality outcomes. The platform wraps these pieces in a modular system with a public interface and documented API. That matters because the goal is not only a research score; it is a tool that reviewers can use for self-checking, editors can use for triage, and researchers can extend when better quality measures appear.
mech: The input is a peer review, likely together with metadata or structured fields available to the review platform, although the abstract only names the review-quality target rather than every input column. PeeriScope first turns the review into structured features: measurable signals that can be handled consistently across many reviews. These features might represent surface and organization properties, but the abstract does not list the exact feature set. Next, the system applies assessments guided by a rubric. A rubric is a written scoring guide: it breaks the vague word "quality" into dimensions that can be checked separately. A large language model is then used as a reading engine that can compare the review text with those criteria and produce dimension-level judgments. The system also uses supervised prediction, meaning it learns from prior examples where some quality signal is already known. That predictor receives the available feature and assessment information and produces a quality estimate or flag useful for triage. The output is not described as a single final number only; the abstract emphasizes multi-dimensional evaluation, interpretability, and extensibility. In practice, the public interface can show assessments to reviewers or editors, while the API lets other systems call the same evaluation pipeline during auditing or research.
math: The main mathematical idea is measurement by decomposition. Instead of pretending review quality is one directly visible fact, the system breaks it into several observable or judgeable dimensions and combines evidence from them. Structured features are a form of counting and categorizing: they convert messy prose into comparable variables. Rubric-guided assessment is scoring under a rulebook: each dimension defines what kind of evidence should raise or lower the judgment. Supervised prediction is learning from examples. It means there is a rule with adjustable settings; the system compares its predicted quality signals with known or accepted examples, then changes the settings so future predictions make fewer mistakes. Probability is also implicit in prediction, because the system must estimate how likely a review is to be high or low quality from partial evidence. The important tradeoff is interpretability versus flexibility. A fixed checklist is easy to inspect but misses meaning. A language model is flexible but can be hard to audit. A trained predictor can combine many signs, but its output needs explanation. PeeriScope's mathematical shape fits the problem because review quality is multi-cue evidence: no single sign proves quality, but several weak signs can become useful when kept separate and compared systematically.
dots: This paper sits in the conference thread where language models are used as workers inside real decision processes, not just as answer generators. In the repo's current data, related peer-review auditing work includes Reviewerly systems such as Peeriscope, Peerispect, and PeerPrism, which connect quality assessment, claim grounding, and human-AI authorship analysis. PeeriScope is the quality-evaluation piece of that larger pressure: scientific venues need machine-readable accountability for reviews. It also connects to ranking and triage, because editors do not need every review inspected with equal urgency; they need likely weak or unusual cases surfaced early. It connects to learning from examples through supervised prediction, and to interpretability because review judgments affect real scholarly decisions. The broader field connection is responsible use of language models in institutional workflows: a model's reading ability is useful only if the system shows criteria, exposes signals, and leaves room for human judgment.
ww: PeeriScope should work better than the naive approaches because review quality leaves traces at different levels. Some traces are structural: whether the review has enough detail, addresses multiple dimensions, or follows expected sections. Some traces are semantic: whether the comments actually engage with the paper's claims and give usable criticism. Some traces are historical: patterns from past labeled or assessed reviews can reveal combinations of signals that tend to match good or poor quality. A checklist only sees the first layer. A free-form model judgment only sees a flexible reading but may drift from venue criteria. A supervised predictor alone can combine evidence but may be hard to interpret. PeeriScope's design triangulates among them. The rubric keeps the model's reading attached to explicit standards; structured features keep part of the evidence inspectable; prediction lets the system learn combinations that humans may not have written as simple rules. The modular design also helps because review standards can change: one part can be adjusted or replaced without treating the entire platform as a black box.
po: The payoff is a deployable way to inspect peer review quality across many reviews without requiring editors to manually audit everything first. Reviewers can use the interface for self-assessment before submitting or revising a review. Editors can use quality signals for triage, deciding which reviews deserve closer human attention before final decisions. Conference or journal operators can run larger audits to understand variability across review processes. Because the system has a documented API and modular design, it can also serve researchers who want to test new quality-evaluation methods rather than rebuild the whole platform.
limits: The abstract does not prove that PeeriScope's judgments are correct across all venues, disciplines, languages, review cultures, or editorial rubrics. Its usefulness depends on the structured features being meaningful, the rubric matching the venue's real standards, and the supervised prediction examples being representative rather than biased toward one review style. Language-model assessments can sound persuasive while still missing domain-specific errors. A quality flag should therefore guide human attention, not replace editorial responsibility. The demo and API show practical availability, but the abstract does not report detailed accuracy, calibration, fairness, or failure-mode evidence.
